headline: Apple emphasizes craft, innovation, and values-driven work; AI language surged dramatically in 2025 after years of minimal mention.
identity: Apple has consistently valued craft excellence, altruism, and inclusion—with particular emphasis on diversity and belonging since 2014. The company's language around DEI strengthened substantially from 2014 onward, peaking around 2021–2022 before stabilizing at elevated levels. However, AI and machine learning language remained nearly absent until 2020, then grew modestly through 2024, before exploding in 2025 with 203 mentions of machine learning and foundation models in job listings alone—a dramatic shift suggesting a major strategic pivot.
fit: You might be a good fit if you are someone who values meticulous attention to detail, believes diversity strengthens innovation, and are drawn to work on foundational AI/ML systems or products that serve billions of users. Apple's language reaches for people who see themselves as part of something larger than themselves and who care about the human impact of technology.

sections.heading: A Long Commitment to Craft and Values
sections.body:
From 1999 onward, Apple's careers copy has centered on the idea of making exceptional products through collaboration and excellence. The company consistently invoked phrases like "shared obsession with getting every last detail right" (2010) and positioned itself as a place where "individual imaginations gather together, committing to the values that lead to great work" (2021). This craft-focused identity remained stable across the entire period, with the craft axis scoring consistently positive from 2010 onward.

Parallel to craft, Apple's altruism language—references to education, environmental responsibility, and social impact—grew substantially. In 1999, altruism scored at –0.19 (zscore); by 2021 it reached 1.47, and has remained elevated through 2026 (0.99). The company began explicitly tying product innovation to human welfare: "For every product we create, we consider the impact it will make — on our customers, on our people, and on our planet" (2020).

sections.heading: DEI Language: Steady Growth, Then Acceleration (2004–2022)
sections.body:
Apple's diversity and inclusion language was sparse in the early 2000s. In 2004, the company mentioned diversity but in neutral, compliance-focused terms. By 2007, language shifted to more aspirational framing: "Apple celebrates diverse experiences and backgrounds" and "diversity provides an environment where each individual can thrive."

The real inflection came in 2014, when CEO Tim Cook's message introduced structural language: "We believe deeply that inclusion inspires innovation" and "our definition of diversity goes far beyond the traditional categories of race, gender, and ethnicity." The inclusion axis jumped from –0.79 (2016) to 1.43 (2021). By 2021–2022, Apple's careers copy was saturated with explicit demographic targets, hiring process reforms, and belonging language: "We're building more diverse interview panels and candidate slates to ensure that diversity is reflected at every stage of the hiring process" (2021). The DEI peak occurred around 2021–2022, then moderated slightly but remained well above pre-2014 levels through 2026.

sections.heading: AI and Machine Learning: Absent Until 2020, Then Explosive in 2025
sections.body:
From 1999 through 2019, Apple's careers pages contained virtually no mentions of AI, machine learning, or related terms. The AI axis registered 0.0 prevalence for every year through 2019.

In 2020, the first signal appeared: 6 AI-related chunks (8% prevalence), mostly in job listings for roles like "Machine Learning Engineer" and "Computer Vision Software Developer." Language remained cautious and technical: mentions of "machine learning," "ML," and "deep learning" appeared in role titles and technical descriptions.

Growth continued modestly through 2021–2024. In 2022, AI prevalence was 5.3%; in 2023, it dropped to 2.8%; in 2024, it fell further to 1.4%—suggesting the company was deprioritizing AI language in its public-facing careers narrative.

Then, in 2025, the shift became dramatic. AI prevalence jumped to 19.7%—a 14-fold increase from 2024. The 2025 data shows 23 AI-related chunks across 117 total chunks, with 203 mentions of machine learning terms in job listings alone. New language appeared: "foundation models," "generative AI," "LLMs," and "multimodal foundation models." Job titles shifted to "AIML - Machine Learning Engineer, Foundation Models" and "Machine Learning Researcher, Multimodal Foundation Models." The tone remained technical but the volume and prominence were unprecedented.

In 2026, prevalence remained elevated at 21.1%, suggesting this is not a temporary spike but a sustained strategic emphasis.

sections.heading: Stability in Performance and Meritocracy Language
sections.body: Throughout the period, Apple's language around performance and meritocracy remained relatively stable. The company consistently emphasized hiring "the best," rewarding "bright, original thinking," and creating environments where "experts lead experts." Performance language scored highest in 2020 (zscore 1.27) and 2019 (1.13), but remained positive across most years. Meritocracy language similarly stayed consistent, with the company framing diversity not as a constraint on excellence but as essential to it: "We know that differences in our backgrounds, identities, and the way we think make our teams stronger and more innovative" (2022).

sections.heading: Wellbeing and Community: Recent Emphasis on Belonging
sections.body: Wellbeing language in Apple's careers copy remained modest through the 2010s but accelerated notably from 2021 onward. In 2023, wellbeing scored 1.72 (zscore), driven by expanded language around mental health, Veterans' benefits, and community: "Our comprehensive benefits are designed to help every Apple employee and their family feel healthy, supported, and secure" (2023). By 2025, wellbeing remained elevated at 1.77, with sustained emphasis on belonging and support systems. This suggests Apple is increasingly framing employment not just as work but as membership in a community with institutional care.
